content: Veterinarians are at risk of infection due to their close contact with infected animals. Healthcare workers are particularly vulnerable to acquiring infections while providing intensive care to patients. In the past, infections have been transmitted to surgeons operating on undiagnosed patients. Mode of Transmission The primary mode of transmission is through direct contact with the blood or tissues of infected livestock, such as sheep, goats, or cattle, as well as through tick bites. Clinical Signs and Symptoms The incubation period is typically 1–3 days following a tick bite or 5–6 days after contact with infected blood or tissues. Symptoms include a sudden onset of high fever, chills, headache, dizziness, and muscle pain. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are common. Patients may exhibit flushed faces and necks, congested conjunctiva, and frequent bleeding from the nose, gums, kidneys, and gastric mucosa. Survivors often experience extreme weakness, sweating, headache, and malaise. Treatment While antiviral agents have shown some benefit in treating Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF), general supportive therapy remains the cornerstone of patient management. Prevention and Control Use insect repellents containing DEET to prevent tick bites. Livestock workers should wear gloves and protective clothing. Avoid contact with the blood and bodily fluids of sick livestock or patients. Adhere strictly to infection-control precautions in healthcare settings. No vaccine exists for human or animal use. Public education on tick bite prevention and personal protection is essential. Dengue Fever Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection that has become a significant global public health concern, particularly in tropical and subtropical climates. It is most prevalent in urban and semi-urban areas. Over the past five decades, dengue cases have increased 30-fold globally, with an estimated 50–100 million new infections annually in over 100 endemic countries. Severe dengue, a potentially fatal complication, was first recognized in the 1950s during outbreaks in the Philippines and Thailand. Today, it is a leading cause of hospitalization and death in many Asian countries. Transmission Dengue viruses are transmitted to humans through the bite of infected female Aedes mosquitoes, which acquire the virus by feeding on an infected person. These mosquitoes bite during the daytime. Clinical Signs and Symptoms The incubation period is 4–6 days after a mosquito bite. Dengue fever presents as a severe flu-like illness, with symptoms including high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, and rash. Infants and young children may experience fever with rash, while older children and adults typically have an abrupt onset of high fever and other symptoms. Treatment There is no specific drug or vaccine for dengue. Paracetamol is recommended to reduce fever and alleviate joint pain, while aspirin should be avoided due to the risk of bleeding. Intravenous fluids are crucial for managing severe cases. Prevention and Control Prevent mosquito breeding by draining stagnant water from containers such as tanks, barrels, and buckets. Use insecticides like temephos to prevent larvae development in water that cannot be drained. Wear long-sleeved clothing and use mosquito repellents. Use mosquito coils and electric vapor mats during the daytime to prevent bites. Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) Ebola virus disease is a severe and often fatal illness in humans, with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. The disease first appeared in 1976 in simultaneous outbreaks in Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The virus is transmitted to humans from wild animals and spreads through human-to-human transmission. Transmission Ebola is introduced into the human population through close contact with the blood, secretions, or bodily fluids of infected animals, such as chimpanzees, gorillas, fruit bats, and monkeys. Human-to-human transmission occurs through direct contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated environments. Burial ceremonies involving direct contact with the deceased can also contribute to transmission. Clinical Signs and Symptoms EVD is characterized by the sudden onset of fever, intense weakness, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat, followed by vomiting, diarrhea, rash, and impaired kidney and liver function. In some cases, internal and external bleeding occurs. The incubation period ranges from 2 to 21 days. Treatment Severely ill patients require intensive supportive care, including rehydration with oral or intravenous fluids. No licensed specific treatment or vaccine is currently available. Healthcare workers should consistently apply standard precautions, including hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, and the use of personal protective equipment. Samples from suspected cases should be handled by trained staff in equipped laboratories. Hantavirus Hantavirus is an emerging viral disease transmitted to humans through rodents. Unlike other Bunyaviridae viruses, hantaviruses are spread through inhalation of aerosols from infected rodent feces. The disease can manifest as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), both of which can be fatal. Transmission Hantavirus is primarily transmitted through inhalation of aerosols from rodent urine or feces, particularly during the dry summer season. Human-to-human transmission is rare but possible. Clinical Signs and Symptoms The incubation period is typically 2–3 weeks. HFRS affects the kidneys and presents with high fever, chills, and abdominal pain, often accompanied by bleeding and impaired kidney function. HPS affects the lungs and is characterized by acute respiratory distress following an initial period of fever, aches, and cough. HPS has a fatality rate of up to 50%. Treatment There are no effective antiviral drugs for hantavirus infections. Treatment is supportive, focusing on managing shock syndrome and providing intensive care when necessary. Prevention and Control Wear protective clothing and avoid inhaling dust or aerosols when cleaning rodent-infested areas. Eliminate rodents from homes and prevent re-entry. Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) HFMD is a common viral disease that primarily affects children under 10 years old, especially those under 5. It is highly contagious and often spreads in kindergartens and schools. Transmission The virus is transmitted through direct contact with nasal and throat secretions, saliva, blister fluid, or stool of infected individuals. Patients are most infectious during the febrile stage. Clinical Signs and Symptoms The incubation period is 3–7 days. HFMD is usually mild and self-limiting, with symptoms including fluid-filled blisters on the hands, feet, and inside the mouth, as well as dehydration due to fever and poor fluid intake. However, outbreaks caused by enterovirus 71 (EV71) have been associated with severe complications such as meningitis, pneumonia, and myocarditis, leading to significant mortality. Treatment Treatment is symptomatic and supportive. Prevention and Control Wash hands thoroughly with soap or use alcohol-based sanitizers. Disinfect contaminated surfaces and items, including toys. Avoid close contact with infected individuals. Promote good hygiene practices in schools and keep sick children away from public places. Japanese Encephalitis (JE) Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne viral disease that primarily affects children in endemic areas. The case fatality rate can reach 25–30%, and 30–50% of survivors suffer long-term neurological damage. Transmission JE outbreaks occur during the rainy season in paddy-growing areas with stagnant water, which serves as breeding grounds for mosquitoes. The virus circulates in birds and amplifies in pigs, which infect mosquitoes that bite humans. Clinical Signs and Symptoms The incubation period is 5–15 days. Symptoms include high fever, stiff neck, coma, tremors, and convulsions, particularly in infants. JE can be clinically confused with cerebral malaria, meningitis, and other viral infections. Treatment There is no specific treatment for JE. Supportive care and good nursing can significantly reduce mortality. Prevention and Control Prevent mosquito bites by using repellents, wearing protective clothing, and eliminating mosquito breeding sites.
